Modest
MOD-est
adj. (orderly; well-arranged; becoming)
Greek kosmios, from kosmos, order or arrangement — well-ordered, seemly, of a piece. The same root gives the English cosmos and cosmetic. Latin modestus, keeping within measure, from modus, a measure.

Biblical Definition

In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array. The Greek word is kosmios, well-ordered, and the verb Paul uses for adorn is from the same root — a Christian woman is to order herself in ordered dress. The instruction is not primarily about how much cloth is present. Paul's four examples are broided hair, gold, pearls, and costly array, and every one of them concerns expense and display rather than exposure. The context is public worship, and the concern is a woman turning the assembly into an occasion for showing her wealth. That is why he pairs modesty with shamefacedness — a proper reverence and reserve — and sobriety, soundness of mind. Peter makes the same point from the same angle: let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; but let it be the hidden man of the heart. Neither apostle forbids clothing or ornament as such; both relocate the adorning. And Paul finishes the sentence by naming what should be conspicuous instead: which becometh women professing godliness, with good works. The dictionary holds the plain sense — immodesty of exposure is genuinely condemned in Scripture — while insisting that Paul's own emphasis here falls where he put it, on display, expense, and the ordering of a life.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): restrained by a sense of propriety; not forward or bold; not excessive or extreme; moderate; decent.

expand to see more

MODEST, a. Properly, restrained by a sense of propriety; hence, not forward or bold; not presumptuous or arrogant; not boastful.

MODEST, a. Not loose; not lewd; as a modest woman.

MODEST, a. Moderate; not excessive or extreme; not extravagant; as a modest request; modest apparel.

SOBRIETY, n. Habitual soberness or temperance; freedom from inordinate passion; calmness; seriousness.

APPAREL, n. Clothing; vesture; garments; dress.

Key Scripture

1 Timothy 2:9 — "In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;"

1 Timothy 2:10 — "But (which becometh women professing godliness) with good works."

1 Peter 3:3 — "Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;"

1 Peter 3:4 — "But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price."

Modern Corruption

Modesty is dismissed in the wider culture as an instrument of control, and reduced within the churches to a hemline rule; Paul's word means well-ordered, and his own examples concern display and expense.

expand to see more

The cultural rejection of modesty treats any standard of dress as an imposition on women and a transfer of responsibility for men's sin. Scripture assigns that responsibility squarely to the man — whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart — and the dictionary does not shift it. But the apostolic instruction still stands, and it is addressed to women as an instruction about their own adorning before God in the assembly. Both things are true at once, and a church that can only say one of them will mislead somebody.

The error inside the churches is to reduce kosmios to a measurement, producing rules about hemlines and necklines that Paul does not give and missing the ones he does. His four examples — broided hair, gold, pearls, costly array — are about conspicuous expense, which means a congregation policing modesty while admiring wealth has inverted the text. The word means well-ordered. It reaches a woman's whole bearing, her speech and her spending as much as her dress, and Paul's positive command is what a watching church should actually notice: good works, becoming women professing godliness.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kosmios (G2887), orderly, well-arranged; kosmeo (G2885), to adorn or set in order; aidos (G127), shamefacedness or reverence; sophrosune (G4997), soundness of mind, sobriety.

expand to see more

Greek kosmios (G2887) — well-ordered, seemly; rendered modest, and of good behaviour of an elder at 1 Timothy 3:2.

Greek kosmeo (G2885) — to arrange, to adorn; the verb rendered adorn, from the same root.

Greek aidos (G127) — a sense of shame, reverence, modesty of bearing; rendered shamefacedness.

Greek sophrosune (G4997) — soundness of mind, self-control; rendered sobriety.

Greek katastole (G2689) — a garment let down, deportment; rendered apparel.

Usage

"“adorn themselves in modest apparel” — ordered dress, from the word for order."

"“not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls” — the examples concern display and expense."

"“with good works” — the adorning Paul commands instead."
